newsitem.title: USA: St. Barbara Mines control may change.
newsitem.headline: St. Barbara Mines control may change.

text.p: The offer for sale of a controlling shareholding in Australian gold miner, St. Barbara Mines Ltd, may enable a larger mining house to gain management control of an existing gold producer with record output of 33,248 ounces in the March 1997 quarter, St. Barbara Mines chairman, Peter Jones, said in an interview in New York.

"The major influence on public perception of St. Barbara has been arguments within the board between the company's two major shareholders, but that's moving towards some resolution, as both of them have got their shareholdings up for sale and, both of them have publicly said they are going to stand down," Jones said.
St. Barbara's former chairman, Alan Birchmore, and a current director, Ross Atkins, currently own about 46 percent of St. Barbara through Bengal Star Pty Ltd.
St. Barbara has about 228 million shares on issue, after a recent issue 15 million shares at A$0.65 a share to Normandy Mining Ltd of Australia which raised A$9.75 million.
A further 25 percent is held by institutional shareholders with U.S. institutions holding about 12 pct, Jones said.

"The controlling shareholding would be an attractive block of stock to a major mining house who wanted significant stake and management rights in an already up-and-running mining operation with considerable potential," Jones said.
In the nine months ended March 1997, St. Barbara had produced 102,184 ounces of gold at an average cash cost of A$397 an ounce, Jones said.
As of March 31, 1997 forward sales totalled 76,208 ounces at average price of A$568 an ounce, with delivery dates out to March 1998.
The Australian dollar price of gold Wednesday was around A$449 an ounce, after seeing a 10 year low in May at A$435.

"Atkins has said publicly he is getting a merchant bank to call tender for his stock, and I don't know what price he will accept, but it's true this represents an overhang over the share price," Jones said.
St. Barbara's share price slid to A$0.55 Wednesday, its lowest level since April 1993, after seeing a high at A$2.60 in March 1994.
Last month St. Barbara announced a joint venture with Normandy Mining Ltd of Australia to develop a prospect in the Cue district of Western Australia.
St. Barbara will have a 30 pct interest and Normandy a 70 pct stake in the so-called "Big Bell Cuddingwarra Consolidated Joint Venture".
Normandy will be the operator of the venture and has been invited to nominate a director to the St. Barbara board.

The assets of the venture will comprise Normandy's Big Bell gold mine and treatment plant which has a capacity of three million tonnes per year, plus St. Barbara's Cuddingwarra gold resource and combined exploration tenements within about 60 kilometres of the plant totalling more than 1,000 sq.km.

Cuddingwarra is expected to be in production within a year at up to 1.3 million tonnes of ore per annum, producing more than 225,000 ounces of gold per year, of which about 67,000 ounces would be attributable to St. Barbara.
At full production, overall cash costs for the Big Bell Cuddingwarra project are expected to be around A$350 per ounce, Jones said.
St. Barbara had proven and probable gold reserves of 1.3 million ounces, according to the June 1996 annual report.
"Asset values of producing gold mines in Australia are in general undervalued compared to those in the U.S. and Canada," Jones claimed.

"The falling price of gold is exacerbating that situation and may result in a shakeout in gold mining in Australia, which provides opportunities for the merging of projects and an opportunity for investors from U.S. to get into projects that may have a lower risk than those in other parts of the world such as Indonesia," he said.
